title: Switching to bass violin and playing left-handed
summary: His guitar was stolen during the Depression so he used his father's bass; he restrings it left-handed.

story.theme_name: Drummers and drumming: who played what, and how
story.community_name: Bass players: lineage, tone and technique

blocks.x: Yes, I did. It was by force that I had to do so because my guitar was stolen from me. That same guitar that you see over there.

And the depression had struck rather hard and I wasn't in position then to buy another instrument. And I had my father's instrument, a bass violin. And I said, I had always played on the bass violin. From a child, he stood me on a stool and showed me how the bass was supposed to be fingered.
He wasn't left handed by the way.
No, he was right handed. My mother's left handed. And one of my sisters is left handed. Yeah. My nephew, he's a dentist, he's left handed.
I never noticed. Do you tune your...
It's re-strung. It's strung just the opposite way. You string it up. It's strung for me just as a right hand man would have his strung from him, but it's in the reverse order.
There's a white bass player here, Sherwood Maginapain, pretty good player. You've probably seen him someplace. He plays left handed, but he doesn't bother to re-string his. He plays on...
Just like a right hand man would string his.
He picks up anybody's bass and plays it left handed.

Well, I do that sometimes if I'm out around musicians. You can do it, huh? Really? Yes. If I'm around musicians and they'll ask me to play, I'll first say that, well I can't play because your bass is strung backwards. And then I'll eventually go there. Because I like to play. I like to play both of the instruments.
As long as you don't have to play a whole chord I guess, it's a stick to one string at a time, you can think of a bit more and do it.
But my guitar was stolen from me and during that time the banjos had almost become obsolete around 35. Yes, that's right. And that forced me to play bass violin.
